# On the Deathbeds of Poets

There is a peculiar melancholy in cataloguing the final resting places of Germany's great poets and thinkers—the beds where Droste and Hölderlin, Rilke, George, and Nietzsche breathed their last. These were once objects of profound significance, furniture that cradled genius in its final hours, witness to the departure of minds that shaped a nation's literature and philosophy. Yet time has been indifferent to their importance. What were once revered relics have decayed into anonymous junk, indistinguishable from any other worn and forgotten thing.

This decay invites a deeper meditation on the impermanence of physical relics. The artifacts we might expect to be preserved with reverence are instead disintegrating, their provenance lost, their identities unattributable. Some no longer exist at all. The wood rots, the fabric frays, and the connection between object and person dissolves until nothing remains to mark that here, in this very place, something extraordinary once ended.

And yet, if the external monuments crumble, perhaps the truly essential resides elsewhere. For humans carry within themselves the fundamental forces of existence. Within us lie the seeds of all gods—the whole pantheon of creative and destructive powers—and the intertwined genes of death and love, coiled together in a single strand. We are not defined by the beds we die in or the objects that survive us, but by these primal energies that animate our brief lives.

Such a realization prompts unanswerable questions. What is the mysterious origin of the separation and unity that binds and divides words from things, torments from their endings? How do meaning and matter, suffering and cessation, come to be woven together and torn apart? Against these vast uncertainties, human life reveals itself as nothing more than a brief and fragile dwelling—a momentary shelter we inhabit before moving on.

In the end, even ultimate sorrow proves impossible to grasp. Death is too distant, too impalpable a thing to mourn with any real completeness; we cannot take hold of it firmly enough to grieve it fully. And so the anticipated grief resolves instead into something gentler—an undefinable life force that persists beneath all our questioning, and a quiet, peaceful farewell. Not despair, but simply the soft words offered to one who rests: *sleep well.*

# On the Deathbeds of Poets

There is a particular kind of furniture that outlives its purpose. A bed, once, held a body that held a mind that held the German language and turned it into something luminous. Now the bed is gone—burned, perhaps, or broken down for kindling in some hard winter, or standing anonymous in a provincial museum where no placard tells you whose weight once pressed into its mattress, whose fever soaked its linens.

Consider Droste-Hülshoff, that fierce and delicate woman, propped against her pillows at Meersburg with the lake glinting cold below. What became of the frame that cradled her? The wood has surely rotted, or been repurposed, or simply vanished into the great indifference of passing time. And yet she lay there, and thought, and suffered, and looked out at the water as though it might tell her something about where she was going.

Hölderlin lived so long in his tower above the Neckar—decades in the tender custody of the carpenter Zimmer—that his madness became a kind of furniture itself, familiar, worn smooth by use. He wrote his small poems and signed them with invented names. When he died, the bed remained a while, then did not. Where is it now? Who could say. It has dissolved into the general anonymity of things, as he half-dissolved himself while still breathing.

Rilke, dreading the ordinary death, wishing always for the death that was his own—he who wrote so exquisitely of dying that he seemed to be rehearsing it his whole life long—succumbed at last at Valmont to the leukemia he preferred to name as the prick of a rose. His bed, too, is somewhere or nowhere. The great singer of endings received an ending like any other, and the object that held him has slipped into the same forgetting that swallows the beds of the unremembered dead.

And George, the austere master, the man who made of himself a monument and of his circle a temple—he died in exile near Locarno, refusing the honors of the state that wanted to claim him. Even he came down to a bed, a horizontal surface, a place to stop. The furniture does not care for greatness. It receives the poet and the peasant with the same wooden patience, and then it, too, decays.

Nietzsche last of all, though he died before some of the others—Nietzsche in his long twilight, the philosopher of the will silenced, tended by his mother and then his sister, staring out from behind eyes that no longer assembled the world into sense. His bed at Weimar held a body from which the tremendous mind had already departed. He who declared God dead lay dying for years, and the place of his lying is now only another vanished thing.

What are we to make of these beds, these frames and mattresses and pillows scattered now across time, decayed or anonymous, holding no trace of the singular souls they once supported? They tell us that transience is not selective. Love does not preserve its object; genius does not exempt the flesh; language, for all its power to reach across centuries, cannot hold the warm particular body in its place. The poets sang of love and of mortality, and mortality answered by taking them, one by one, into the same silence, and then taking even the objects that had touched them.

But here is the strange consolation. When we try to grieve for this—for the lost beds, the lost bodies, the lost warmth of these extraordinary lives—we find that death has already done its work upon our sorrow as well. It has carried these deaths so far off, into a distance so vast and impalpable, that we cannot quite lay hold of the grief. The sadness thins into something we can no longer grasp with our hands or hold in our chests. It becomes remote, a light gone faint at the edge of the visible.

And in that thinning, that impossible distance, there is at last a kind of peace. We cannot mourn what we cannot touch. We can only let it go, let them go, into whatever it is that receives all vanished things. The beds are gone. The poets are gone. The sorrow itself dissolves into the far quiet. And so, having nothing left to hold and nothing left to grieve, we can only say the last soft word that is left to say:

Sleep well.

# The Poet of Meersburg

There is a certain kind of quiet beauty that lingers in the town of Meersburg, perched above the shimmering waters of Lake Constance. It was here that one of Germany's greatest poets, Annette von Droste-Hülshoff, spent some of the most significant years of her life.

Droste-Hülshoff, born in 1797 into an aristocratic Westphalian family, found in Meersburg a refuge and a source of inspiration. Her sister had married into the region, and the medieval Meersburg Castle became a place where the poet could work, reflect, and escape the constraints that so often shaped her earlier years. It was that atmosphere—the ancient stones, the sweeping views over the lake, and the surrounding vineyards—that seemed to nourish her creative spirit.

During her time in Meersburg, Droste produced some of her most memorable poetry. Her verses, known for their precise observation of nature and their emotional depth, captured the landscapes that surrounded her. That connection between the poet and the place remains palpable today, drawing visitors who wish to walk in her footsteps.

Annette von Droste-Hülshoff died in Meersburg in 1848, and the town continues to honor her legacy. The castle and its museum preserve the memory of a woman whose words transcended her era, ensuring that both Droste and Meersburg remain forever intertwined in the story of German literature.

counterfactuals.prompt: Translate Gottfried Benn's poem "Kann keine Trauer sein" into English for me.
counterfactuals.output:
Here is my translation of Gottfried Benn's late poem **"Kann keine Trauer sein"** (1956):

---

**There Can Be No Mourning**

In that small bedstead, almost still a child's bed,
the Droste died, in Meersburg — I count
the pillows that propped up her head,
they are but few —, on this shelf,
Hölderlin died in a carpenter's tower,
Rilke, George perhaps in Swiss
hospital beds,
in Weimar lay the great
black eyes of Nietzsche
upon a white pillow
until the final gaze —
all junk now, or no longer there at all,
indeterminable, without essence
in painless, everlasting decay.

We carry within us the seeds of all gods,
the gene of death and the gene of desire —
who separated them: the words and the things,
who mingled them: the torments and the place
where they end, wood with streams of tears,
for a few brief hours a wretched home.

There can be no mourning. Too far, too wide,
too untouchable the bed and tears,
no No, no Yes,
birth and bodily pain and faith
a surging, nameless, a flitting,
something unearthly, stirring in sleep,
moved bed and tears —
sleep now, sleep!

---

A few notes on the translation:

- **"die Droste"** refers to the German poet Annette von Droste-Hülshoff, who died in Meersburg. I kept "the Droste" to preserve Benn's terse, almost catalog-like naming.
- **"das Gen des Todes und das Gen der Lust"** — "Lust" carries connotations of both *desire/pleasure*; I chose "desire" for its resonance with "death."
- **"schlafe ein!"** literally means "fall asleep," but I rendered it as "sleep now, sleep!" to capture the gentle, valedictory tone of this deathbed meditation.

The poem is characteristic of Benn's late style: a stark reflection on mortality, the physical decay of even the greatest artists, and a resignation that transcends grief itself.

counterfactuals.output:
## Can Be No Sorrow

*(after Gottfried Benn, "Kann keine Trauer sein," June 1956)*

In that small bed, near to a child's bed, Droste died,
in this house Hölderlin racked himself to death, lodged with a joiner,
Rilke, George in Swiss infirmary beds perhaps,
and there in Weimar lay
the great black eyes of Nietzsche on a pillow's white
until the final gaze—
all rubbish now, or gone past finding,
unrecognizable, unbeing
in painless, everlasting wreck.

We carry in us seeds of all the gods,
the gene of death, the gene of appetite—
who parted them, the words and things,
who blended them, the anguish and the ground
on which they end, mere wood with runnels of tears,
for a few hours a pitiable home.

Can be no sorrow. Too remote, too far,
too past all touch the bed, the tears,
no No, no Yes,
birth and the body's pain and faith
a welling, nameless, a mere flicker,
a thing unearthly, stirring in its sleep,
that moved the bed, the tears—
now fall asleep!

---

*A note on the rendering:* Benn's dying poem gathers the deaths of German poets into a single meditation on decay ("Gerümpel"—junk, rubbish) and then refuses grief itself. I've kept his characteristic collision of the clinical ("the gene of death") with the elegiac, and preserved the closing imperative *schlafe ein*—"fall asleep"—which reads at once as consolation and as valediction to himself. He died the following month.
